parsed.explanation: No trans-specific criminal offence, border/facility/custody restriction, or documented police targeting of visitors is documented; same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 1998. Article 99 criminalises incitement to violence/hatred on gender-identity grounds, prejudice is an aggravating factor, and conversion practices are banned. The discounts are inconsistent enforcement (no action on some clergy incitement and capital attacks, failure to establish hate motive), absence of gender identity from equal-treatment grounds, no national gender-recognition law in force, and a fragmented framework. Resident recognition gaps are climate signals, not direct visitor exposure. Overall: reduced-risk, with recourse uneven in practice.

entry_documents.protection: No criminalisation of same-sex conduct; no documented entry refusal or document-mismatch practice for foreign visitors.
entry_documents.interaction: Visitor uses home passport; absence of domestic recognition law is not documented to affect foreign documents.

federal_state_facilities.protection: One part operates its own recognition process including non-binary identities; national bill pending since 2022.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Subnational recognition difference is administrative; no facility-access rule for visitors is documented in either part.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Enforcement of hate-speech and hate-crime provisions is inconsistent; some clergy incitement drew no action.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Article 99 punishes incitement to violence/hatred on sexual-orientation/gender-identity grounds up to three years; prejudice is an aggravating factor; conversion practices banned in 2023.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Paper protections coexist with documented non-enforcement, weakening recourse for an outed visitor.

minors_guardians.interaction: Recognition legislation for adults and minors was described as in preparation in 2019 but no law is in force nationally; no visitor minor restriction is documented.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: February 2019 capital attack on a gay man: police failed to establish hate motive; a second incident four months later drew no police action. No trans-specific visitor violence documented.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Eleven complaints examined in 2015 and five prosecutions pending; prison guards received two-day training in 2023 after complaints.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Inconsistent police response is the main street-level risk if an outed visitor is assaulted.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: No general prohibition of discrimination based on gender identity; employment law covers sexual orientation only; framework assessed as fragmented.
remedies_unknowns.protection: State accepted all SOGIESC recommendations at 2019 review; hate-speech and aggravating-factor laws enacted.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Protections are real but incomplete and unevenly enforced; no anti-homophobia action plan exists.

anchor_checks.comparison: Similar in that remedies exist but are uneven; higher here because no documented visitor detention, care refusal, or document-mismatch questioning, whereas 0.65-B centres on a clinic refusal later overturned.

Similar: formal protections with discretionary gaps and slow/uneven enforcement, brief friction rather than custody. Lower here because gender identity is absent from equal-treatment grounds and some attacks drew no police action.

Lower than 0.85-A: that anchor has explicit gender-identity coverage across services and independent oversight with apologies/compensation; here coverage is fragmented, enforcement is documented as inconsistent, and no gender-recognition law is in force.

parsed.synthesis: Combined regime: no traveller-facing criminalisation, facility ban, border screening, or custody exposure is documented, so the worst documented feature is tier-3 societal/institutional thinness — inconsistent hate-crime enforcement and missing gender-identity discrimination protection — rather than tier-1 state-imposed exposure. Statutory protections (Article 99, aggravating factor, conversion ban) mitigate but are documented as unevenly applied, including impunity for clergy incitement. Absence of domestic recognition does not directly expose a visitor on a home passport, but completes a picture of incomplete institutional protection. This sits above the 0.65 friction-with-working-remedy tier and below the 0.85 explicit-protection tier.
